runs.text: The authors did not run the Cyrene-based separation at room temperature as the working condition. The separation was done hot, because PVDF dissolves in Cyrene only at elevated temperature: it was barely soluble below the higher test temperature.
Room temperature played other roles. The hot supernatant was cooled to room temperature on purpose to induce phase separation, so that the PVDF/CB composite could be recovered by filtration.

rendered: The authors did not run the Cyrene-based separation at room temperature as the working condition. The separation was done hot, because PVDF dissolves in Cyrene only at elevated temperature: it was barely soluble below the higher test temperature.[1] Room temperature played other roles. The hot supernatant was cooled to room temperature on purpose to induce phase separation, so that the PVDF/CB composite could be recovered by filtration.[2] Room-temperature filtration was also a comparison case. Cooling the PVDF/Cyrene solution makes PVDF precipitate and gel, so it reprecipitates onto the cathode particles.[3][4] The FTIR PVDF band therefore appears in the room-temperature filtered powder but not in the hot-filtered powder, which shows why the mixture must be kept hot.[5]
